titre: The Peace of Augsburg (1555): One Territory, One Religion, One Prince
accroche: In 1555, the Holy Roman Empire no longer asks each subject to believe as his prince does, but to choose: conform, or leave.
contenu_vulgarise:
On September 25, 1555, in Augsburg, the peace that ended the religious troubles in the Holy Roman Empire was concluded; Ferdinand, brother of Emperor Charles V, had negotiated it on his behalf. The text does not try to reconcile Catholics and Lutherans on the substance: it separates them, territory by territory.

## One Territory, One Faith

The principle adopted holds that each prince of the Empire chooses the religion, Catholic or Lutheran, of his own territory, and that his subjects conform to it. The other confessions, Calvinism foremost, remain outside the peace: the text explicitly excludes them: all others, those who are not adherents of either of the two recognized religions, “are not included in this peace, but shall be altogether excluded from it.” A subject who refuses his prince's religion is not persecuted on the spot: article 24 guarantees him the right to leave with his family, to sell his property, and not to be harmed in his honor, serfs being excluded from this right.

The Latin formula that sums up this principle, *cuius regio, eius religio*, has become, in textbooks, the very name of the Peace of Augsburg. Yet it does not appear in it: the expression is first written down only in 1579, twenty-four years later, according to Bernard Vogler. In 1555, the text lays down the rule; it is not yet summed up in Latin.

## What This Changes

Forty-three years later, the kingdom of France chooses the opposite. The Edict of Nantes, signed by Henry IV in April 1598, does not carve the kingdom into confessional territories: it keeps Catholics and Protestants under a single authority and grants them, within a single space, different rights. Article VI allows Protestants to “live and dwell in all cities and places” of the kingdom without being harassed or compelled in matters of faith; places of security, which the Reformed hold for eight years, guarantee this coexistence by arms rather than by a border.

The two texts answer the same question (how a political power survives a population divided by faith) and answer it in opposite ways. The Empire chooses local homogeneity and individual mobility: no one is forced to change religion, but people are forced to choose between conforming and leaving. France chooses coexistence on the spot, on condition of armed strongholds to hold it together. Neither solution anticipates the other: the Peace of Augsburg excludes Calvinism, which obtains legal recognition only with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, which moreover removes the private exercise of worship from the prince's authority.

repere.texte: The Latin expression cuius regio, eius religio, which is associated with the Peace of Augsburg of 1555, appears in writing only in 1579: twenty-four years after the text it is supposed to sum up.
repere.source: Bernard Vogler, “Le protestantisme dans l'empire après 1555” (“Protestantism in the Empire After 1555”), in L'Édit de Nantes (1598), la France et l'Europe (The Edict of Nantes (1598), France and Europe), ed. Alain Joblin, 1998

carte.punch: The formula that sums up the Peace of Augsburg did not yet exist in 1555.
carte.idee: The Peace of Augsburg (1555) lets each prince of the Holy Roman Empire choose the religion of his territory, Catholic or Lutheran. Its famous formula, cuius regio eius religio, is written down only in 1579. Forty-three years later, the Edict of Nantes chooses the opposite: one kingdom, two religions.
carte.source_courte: B. Vogler, OpenEdition; Edict of Nantes, 1598

quiz.question: Why can the Latin expression cuius regio, eius religio not be the actual text of the 1555 peace?
choix: Because it describes the opposite of the principle actually applied in 1555
Because it originally concerned only the kingdom of France
Because it was written down only in 1579, twenty-four years after the peace
Because the Catholic Church had it removed from the text after it was signed
quiz.explication: According to Vogler, the expression appears in writing only in 1579, twenty-four years after the peace. It does describe the principle applied from 1555, but is not its original wording; it does not concern France, and nothing indicates that it was removed from a text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What can a subject who refuses the religion chosen by his prince do, according to the Peace of Augsburg?
choix: He may leave and sell his property, unless he is a serf
He may freely practice his religion on the spot
He must pay a special tax to stay
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 24 guarantees the right to leave with one's property without being harmed in one's honor, serfs being excluded from this right. There is no mention of execution, of free practice on the spot, or of a special tax.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which confession does the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 explicitly exclude?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text recognizes only Catholicism and Lutheranism; the other confessions, Calvinism included, are excluded from it, and Calvinism obtains legal recognition only with the Peace of Westphalia (1648).
